prompt: You reworded an error message for clarity, and a customer's integration broke because it parsed the old text.
why: With enough users, even undocumented details become part of the contract.
trap: The docs never promised the text; users relied on it anyway.

prompt: A storage upgrade changed the order in which list results come back. The docs never promised an order, yet dozens of clients broke.
why: Observable behavior becomes depended on. Randomize unpromised orderings early or document them.
trap: Being technically right per the docs doesn't prevent the breakage.

prompt: Making an endpoint faster broke a client that had been relying on it taking at least 200 ms.
tells: Making an endpoint faster broke a client
why: Even performance is observable behavior that someone will depend on.
trap: It sounds absurd, which is exactly the point of the law.

prompt: Removing a field marked "internal, do not use" from an API response breaks 30 external customers.
why: If it's visible, someone depends on it. Plan deprecations with usage data and notice.
trap: Labels don't stop dependencies; visibility creates them.

prompt: A language update randomized hash map iteration order, and several test suites that compared printed maps started failing.
why: Iteration order was never promised, but enough users depended on it.
trap: Some languages randomize it on purpose to stop people from depending on it.

prompt: A library raised its default timeout from 5 to 30 seconds, and a client's retry logic, built around failing in 5, started piling up stuck requests.
why: An undocumented default became part of the contract for someone.
trap: The pile-up is queueing, but the root is a behavior change users depended on.

prompt: A spreadsheet program still treats 1900 as a leap year because fixing it would break decades of files that rely on the wrong date math.
tells: still treats 1900 as a leap year
why: With enough users, even a bug becomes a feature someone depends on.
trap: Keeping a known bug looks strange until you count who'd break.

prompt: A proxy started sending HTTP headers in lowercase, which the spec allows, and a partner's integration broke because it matched exact casing.
why: Spec-compliant change, yet someone depended on the observable behavior.
trap: Being correct by the spec doesn't protect you from observed behavior.
